questions.explain: The chapter defines an embedding as a fixed-length array of floats, typically 384 to 3,072 dimensions, where each dimension captures a latent feature learned during model training.
options: A full-text catalog that maps keywords to document IDs
A sparse TF-IDF vector where most dimensions are zero
A fixed-length array of floating-point numbers, typically 384 to 3,072 dimensions depending on the model
An encrypted hash that can be reversed to recover the original content
questions.q: According to Chapter 1, what exactly is an embedding?

questions.explain: 4 bytes per float × 1,536 dimensions = 6,144 bytes ≈ 6 KB per row, so one million vectors need roughly 6 GB of raw storage before indexes.
options: About 6 KB (4 bytes × 1,536 = 6,144 bytes)
About 64 KB
About 1.5 KB
About 600 bytes
questions.q: The chapter states that a 1,536-dimension float32 embedding occupies about how much raw storage?

questions.explain: The embedding space is model-specific; vectors from text-embedding-3-small and all-MiniLM-L6-v2 cannot be compared, so a model upgrade means re-embedding everything.
options: Nothing — embeddings are portable across models
Divide old vectors by the new model's dimension count
Store both versions and let the optimizer pick at query time
Re-embed the entire dataset, because vectors from different models live in different coordinate spaces and cannot be compared
questions.q: What must you do when you upgrade your embedding model, according to the chapter?

questions.explain: A B-tree works because values have a total ordering; vector similarity is geometric, so finding the closest of 10 million vectors requires distance to every candidate unless a specialized structure is used.
options: B-trees cannot store floating-point numbers
Vector similarity has no total ordering, so a query cannot carve off a predictable subtree the way WHERE price < 100 does
Embeddings exceed the 900-byte index key limit
B-tree pages cannot be stored on SSDs
questions.q: Why can't a B-tree index speed up nearest-neighbor vector search?

questions.explain: DiskANN — the graph-based ANN algorithm behind SQL Server 2025's native vector index — is compared with HNSW, the index inside Qdrant, Weaviate, and other dedicated engines; both offer O(log n) queries at 95–99% recall.
options: B-tree (SQL Server) vs. hash index (dedicated engines)
HNSW (SQL Server) vs. DiskANN (dedicated engines)
DiskANN (SQL Server 2025) vs. HNSW (engines like Qdrant and Weaviate)
Full-text index (SQL Server) vs. inverted index (dedicated engines)
